Elephants in Thailand 
3
The Asian elephant is a smaller cousin of the  
African elephant, with relatively smaller ears.  
It is the largest terrestrial mammal in Asia. 
The elephant’s massive size and strength  
made it a reliable beast of burden. It is  
a national symbol of Thailand and has  
served many roles in that country’s  
long history. It has been used in timber  
logging, as a war machine and in  
processions and ceremonies. 
In 2010, it was estimated that only  
about 2 000 wild elephants remained in  
the forests of Thailand. It was estimated  
there were approximately 3 000  
domesticated elephants. 
Today, domesticated elephants are  
more likely to be seen carrying tourists  
or performing in some form of  
entertainment than working in  
the jungle or on farms.
1 
Around 1900 it was estimated that there were at least 100 000 domesticated elephants 
working in Thailand. By 1952, that number had dropped to around 13 400. 
 
In 2010, it was estimated that there were only 3 000 domesticated elephants and  
2 000 wild elephants in Thailand.
 
Express the number of domesticated elephants in Thailand in 2010 as a percentage of 
a the number of domesticated elephants in 1900. 
b the number of domesticated elephants in 1952.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
c the total number of elephants in 2010.
d the number of wild elephants in 2010.
2 
Tan is a mahout (an elephant handler). He is 1.68 m tall and has a mass of 68 kg. 
 
His elephant is 2.8 m tall and has a mass of 4.76 tonnes (4 760 kg).
a Express Tan’s height as a percentage of the height of his elephant. 
b Express Tan’s mass as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
3 
Tan’s elephant eats around 135 kg of plant matter each day. 
 
Express this as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.

Once they are born, baby elephants enjoy a 3 to 5 year childhood before their training begins. 
They learn to push, carry and stack logs as well as how to walk in a procession.  
Working elephants have a career of about 50 years. 
4 
Tan began training his elephant when it was 4 years old.  
The training took 5 years.  
Tan and the elephant then began work.  
His elephant is now 25 years old.
a How many years has the elephant been working? 
b What percentage of its life did the elephant spend in training? 
c What percentage of the elephant’s life has it been working? 
5 
The law in Thailand requires working elephants to be retired at age 61 after working  
for 50 years. They are usually released into the wild. 
 
An elephant at a sanctuary is 72 years old. 
 
What percentage of its life did the elephant spend working?  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
Each year, the town of Surin in north-eastern Thailand hosts an Elephant Round-up Festival. 
More than 300 domesticated elephants are brought to the town by their mahouts.  
The festival lasts 10 days. The elephants demonstrate their skills and participate in parades 
and battle re-enactments. 
6 
The average elephant drinks 160 litres of water each day. 
a How many kilolitres of water are needed for each elephant for 10 days? 
b How many kilolitres of water are needed for 300 elephants for 10 days? 
7 
The average elephant has a mass of 4 800 kg.  
It eats 130 kg of plants and vegetables each day. 
a What is the total mass of plants and vegetables the average elephant will eat  
during the 10 days of the festival?  
b Express this as a percentage of the mass of the elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
8 
A female elephant stands 2.3 metres in height and has a normal mass of 3.2 tonnes  
(3 200 kg). She gave birth to a baby. Shortly after birth, the baby stood 90 centimetres 
high and had a mass of 90 kg.
a Express the baby’s height as a percentage of its mother’s height.  
Answer correct to the nearest whole number.
b Express the baby’s mass as a percentage of its mother’s mass.  
Answer correct to one decimal place.
9 
A male elephant has a mass of 3.4 tonnes.  
Its brain has a mass of 5 kg. Express this as a percentage of the elephant’s mass.  
Answer correct to two decimal places.

Shinkansen (bullet trains). The first 
bullet train was operated between 
Tokyo and Osaka in 1964, the year the 
Olympic Games were held in Tokyo. 
Today bullet trains run between many 
cities in Japan. On some lines, trains 
run every 5 to 10 minutes.
The fastest trains are called ‘Nozomi’. 
They connect major cities like Tokyo, 
Nagoya, Osaka and Hiroshima, 
making few stops in between. 
1

How long does the journey take?  
Answer in hours and minutes.

b Convert your answer to hours, correct to 2 decimal places.

a distance of 513 kilometres.

Time

a Convert the time to hours, correct to 2 decimal places.

The city of Angkor was the capital of the Khmer 
Empire. Its ruins are located near the modern 
city of Siem Reap in Cambodia.
The temples of Angkor were built during the 
period 802 to 1432. During this time, the 
Khmer Empire was one of the great powers 
of South East Asia. At the height of its power, 
the Khmer Empire ruled over a vast territory 
covering large parts of modern-day Cambodia, 
Laos, Thailand, Myanmar (Burma) and 
southern Vietnam.
Angkor Wat (meaning City Temple) is the 
best known of the temples in this area. It was 
built as a Hindu temple during the reign of 
Suryavarman II (1112 to 1152). It was later 
restored for use as a Buddhist shrine in the  
16th century.
Angkor Wat is surrounded by a moat, 190 metres wide, that forms  
a giant rectangle measuring 1.5 km by 1.3 km. The rectangular wall  
around the enclosure measures 1025 m by 800 m, and has a gate in each side. 
1 
Calculate the perimeter of the moat. 
2 
Calculate the perimeter of the walled enclosure inside the moat. 
3 
What is the area of the enclosure? 
4 
a Calculate the area of the large rectangle, including the moat, in square kilometres.
b Convert your answer to square metres. 
5 
What are the dimensions of the area inside the moat? 
6

consists of three storeys. The corners of the second and third storeys are marked by towers.

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
The Great Wall in northern China is one of the 
great human-made wonders of the world. Like 
a gigantic dragon, the Great Wall winds up and 
down across deserts, grasslands and mountains. 
The first sections were constructed more than 
2 000 years ago by independent kingdoms to 
keep out marauding nomads. These sections 
were later rebuilt and joined together. 
The wall as it is known today dates from the 
Ming Dynasty (1368–1644) when a determined 
effort was made to revitalise the whole project. 
This time, the wall was faced with some 60 
million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs. 
The Great Wall stretched approximately 
8 850 kilometres from east to west. 
Unfortunately, some of the sections are  
now in ruins or have disappeared.
A comprehensive archaeological survey has concluded that the wall of the Ming era  
measured 8 850 km. This is made up of 6 259 km of actual wall, 359 km of trenches  
and 2 232 km of natural defensive barriers such as hills and rivers.
1 
What percentage, correct to 1 decimal place, of the Ming-era wall was
a actual wall?
b trenches?
c natural defensive barriers?
2 
The average height of the Ming-era Great Wall measured  
10.1 metres and the average width was about 4.6 metres.  
Assume the wall was a rectangular prism.  
Use these dimensions to calculate
a the area of a one face of the wall 1 000 metres long.
b the volume of a 1 kilometre section of the wall.  
Answer in cubic metres.
3 
In the Ming era, the wall was faced with approximately  
60 million cubic metres of bricks and stone slabs.  
The length of actual wall was 6 259 kilometres. 
 
What was the average volume of bricks and stone slabs  
used for each kilometre of the wall?  
Answer to the nearest cubic metre.

Made of stone and bricks from the hills, this portion of the Great Wall is 7.8 metres high and  
5 metres wide. The inside has been formed by tamping earth and small stones, which makes 
the wall very firm and strong.

Australia has three time zones (ignoring daylight saving in summer):
• 
 Eastern Standard Time is used in Queensland, New South Wales (excluding Broken Hill), 
Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT.
• 
 Central Standard Time is used in South Australia, the Northern Territory and Broken Hill.
• 
 Western Standard Time is used in Western Australia.
Eastern Standard Time is 30 minutes ahead of Central Standard Time.  
It is 30 minutes earlier in Adelaide than Brisbane. 
Eastern Standard Time is 2 hours ahead of Western Standard Time.  
It is 2 hours earlier in Perth than Brisbane.
Papua New Guinea is also in this time zone.

a Sydney? 
b Darwin?
 
Central Standard Time is 30 minutes behind Eastern Standard Time.  
It is 30 minutes later in Melbourne than Adelaide.

It is 1 hour and 30 minutes earlier in Perth than Adelaide.
Japan, Korea and the eastern part of Indonesia are also in this time zone.

China, Malaysia and the Philippines are also is this time zone.

collections. This year’s Fashion Week is themed ‘Botany’, as a way of emphasising the importance of 
the environment. Eco-friendly products are used throughout the exhibition centre.
Showing off!

‘thread’ in Italian. The WonderDome is hosting this prestigious event. Six runways allow

guests that could sit across all runways per day.

of each of the 4500 fashion buyers.

galleries are generally located in major cities and key regional centres. Important shows are often
